cs-statements.title: What counts as a statement?
cs-statements.body: A proposition is a statement with a definite truth value: true or false. It can be false and still be a proposition.
exampleSteps: It makes a definite claim.
That claim is false, but its truth value is clear.
cs-statements.takeaway: A question or instruction is not a proposition. A claim with an unspecified variable may need more information.

cs-implication.title: When does a rule fail?
cs-implication.body: An implication says: if P is true, Q must be true. To disprove it, find a case where P is true and Q is false.
cs-implication.example: If a number is divisible by 4, it is even.
exampleSteps: 8 is divisible by 4 and is even.
An odd number does not break this rule: its “if” condition is false.
cs-implication.takeaway: A counterexample makes P true and Q false.

cs-converse.title: Can you reverse a rule?
cs-converse.body: The converse swaps a rule’s condition and conclusion. A rule can be true while its converse is false.
cs-converse.example: If a number is divisible by 10, it is divisible by 5.
exampleSteps: The converse says: if divisible by 5, then divisible by 10.
15 satisfies the converse’s condition but not its conclusion.
cs-converse.takeaway: Reversing an implication creates a new claim that needs its own justification.

cs-negation.title: Negate a claim precisely
cs-negation.body: The negation of a claim is true exactly when the original claim is false. To disprove “every”, one exception is enough.
cs-negation.example: Every item in this list is positive.
exampleSteps: Its negation is: at least one item is not positive.
Not positive means zero or negative, not just negative.

ml-components.title: Read a vector
ml-components.body: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. Each component describes one coordinate or feature, and its position matters.
exampleSteps: The first component is 2; the second is −1.
There are three components, so x belongs to a 3-dimensional space.
ml-components.takeaway: Match the component order when comparing vectors or applying model weights.

ml-dot.title: Multiply, then add
ml-dot.body: The dot product multiplies matching components and adds the results. Both vectors must have the same number of components.
exampleSteps: Multiply matching entries: 2 × 3 = 6 and 1 × (−1) = −1.
Add them: a · b = 6 − 1 = 5.
ml-dot.takeaway: The dot product returns one number, not another vector.

ml-angle.title: What does the sign tell you?
ml-angle.body: For two nonzero vectors, the dot product’s sign tells you whether the angle between them is below, equal to, or above 90°.
exampleSteps: Their dot product is 0.
Both vectors are nonzero, so they are perpendicular.
ml-angle.takeaway: Positive: below 90°. Zero: 90°. Negative: above 90°. The angle with a zero vector is undefined.

ml-projection.title: Measure along a direction
ml-projection.body: The dot product with a unit vector gives a signed scalar projection: how much a vector points along that direction.
ml-projection.example: Let x = (3, 4) and unit direction u = (1, 0).
exampleSteps: The signed amount along the horizontal direction is 3.
ml-projection.takeaway: Use a unit direction. A negative projection means the opposite direction.

cs-u1-claims.title: Precise claims and assumptions
cs-u1-claims.body: A predicate becomes true or false when its inputs are fixed. A universal claim concerns every permitted input: one counterexample disproves it, while successful examples alone do not prove it. Unless stated otherwise, arithmetic uses mathematical integers without overflow; ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …}.
cs-u1-claims.example: For an array of length n, P(i, n) describes a valid index.
exampleSteps: P(2, 5) is true because 0 ≤ 2 < 5.
An implication P ⇒ Q lets us conclude Q once P has been established.
cs-u1-claims.takeaway: Check the input domain and the assumptions behind a claim.

cs-u1-direct.title: Direct proofs
cs-u1-direct.body: To prove an implication directly, assume its premise and derive its conclusion using definitions and established facts. Make the assumptions supporting each step explicit.
cs-u1-direct.example: If a = 4k for an integer k, then a + 4 is also a multiple of 4.
exampleSteps: Since k + 1 is an integer, this is an integer multiple of 4.
cs-u1-direct.takeaway: A direct proof connects the premise to the conclusion through justified steps.

cs-u1-contrapositive.title: Converses and contrapositives
cs-u1-contrapositive.body: P ⇒ Q is equivalent to its contrapositive, ¬Q ⇒ ¬P. Reversing it to Q ⇒ P produces the converse, which needs its own justification.
cs-u1-contrapositive.example: A multiple of 10 is a multiple of 5.
exampleSteps: Its contrapositive says: a number not divisible by 5 cannot be divisible by 10.
The converse is different: 5 is divisible by 5 but not by 10.
cs-u1-contrapositive.takeaway: For a contrapositive, negate both statements and reverse their order.

cs-u1-equivalence.title: If and only if
cs-u1-equivalence.body: Proving P ⇔ Q requires both directions. Alternatively, connect the statements through steps that are all reversible.
cs-u1-equivalence.formula: P ⇔ Q: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P
exampleSteps: Subtracting 5 gives x = 4.
Adding 5 reverses the step and gives x + 5 = 9.
cs-u1-equivalence.takeaway: One implication alone does not establish an equivalence.

cs-u1-cases.title: Proof by cases
cs-u1-cases.body: Split the permitted inputs into cases that cover every possibility. Prove the claim in each case; check boundaries carefully.
cs-u1-cases.example: To prove |x| ≥ 0 for real x, split by the sign of x.
exampleSteps: If x ≥ 0, then |x| = x ≥ 0.
If x < 0, then |x| = −x > 0.
cs-u1-cases.takeaway: Correct arguments within incomplete cases do not prove the whole claim.

cs-u1-contradiction.title: Contradiction and proof review
cs-u1-contradiction.body: A contradiction proof assumes the claim is false and derives something impossible. When reviewing any proof, check for circular reasoning and assumptions that do not match the problem.
cs-u1-contradiction.example: A positive real x cannot satisfy x + 1 ≤ x.
exampleSteps: Assume x + 1 ≤ x.
Subtracting x gives 1 ≤ 0, which is impossible.
cs-u1-contradiction.takeaway: A proof must establish its claim under the assumptions of the actual problem.

cs-u2-ordering.title: What well-ordering guarantees
cs-u2-ordering.body: Every nonempty subset of ℕ has a least element. A set is well-ordered when every nonempty subset has a least element. A lower bound need not belong to the set; a minimum must. Throughout this unit, sets use the usual numerical order.
exampleSteps: Three belongs to the set and is no larger than any other member.
Finiteness is not required.
cs-u2-ordering.takeaway: Having a minimum is different from every nonempty subset having a minimum.

cs-u2-minimal.title: The smallest counterexample
cs-u2-minimal.body: To establish P(n) for all n ∈ ℕ, suppose counterexamples exist and choose the smallest one. Derive a contradiction, either by proving it satisfies P, or by finding a smaller counterexample.
cs-u2-minimal.example: If P(0) is already established, a smallest counterexample must be positive.
exampleSteps: Let m be the smallest counterexample.
Every permitted value smaller than m satisfies P.
cs-u2-minimal.takeaway: A smaller value contradicts minimality only if it is also a counterexample.

cs-u2-correctness.title: Proving a counting function correct
cs-u2-correctness.body: Consider a function on finite binary strings. It returns 0 for the empty string; on a prefix followed by bit b, it returns countOnes(prefix) + b. Here b has numerical value 0 or 1. We will prove correctness using the length of a shortest failing input.
exampleSteps: countOnes("") = 0
countOnes(prefix followed by bit b) = countOnes(prefix) + b
cs-u2-correctness.takeaway: Choose the smallest failing length, so every shorter input is handled correctly.

cs-u2-factors.title: Existence of prime factorizations
cs-u2-factors.body: A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. We will use a smallest-counterexample argument to show that every integer greater than 1 is a product of primes. A single prime counts as such a product.
cs-u2-factors.example: This expression writes 42 as a product of primes.
exampleSteps: Each factor is prime.
A prime such as 7 is already a one-factor product of primes.
cs-u2-factors.takeaway: Existence and uniqueness are separate claims.

cs-u2-termination.title: Well-ordering and termination
cs-u2-termination.body: A computation cannot keep strictly decreasing a nonnegative integer forever. A termination argument therefore looks for such a measure. Assume each individual loop iteration finishes; a measure that merely stays the same or decreases is insufficient by itself.
cs-u2-termination.formula: V ∈ ℕ; each step strictly lowers V
cs-u2-termination.example: Removing one item per iteration from a fixed finite queue decreases its remaining length.
exampleSteps: The length is a nonnegative integer.
It decreases by 1 each time an item is removed.
cs-u2-termination.takeaway: The measure’s domain and strict decrease both matter.

cs-u3-conditions.title: Boolean conditions and specifications
cs-u3-conditions.body: AND requires both operands; inclusive OR permits either or both. XOR requires exactly one. P ⇒ Q fails only when P is true and Q is false; it does not assert causation or the converse. P ⇔ Q requires equal truth values. Here all Boolean checks are defined, deterministic and have no side effects. Logical equivalence alone does not justify reordering real code that can throw, mutate state or fail to terminate.
cs-u3-conditions.example: A job may run exactly when capacity C is available and either token T or override O is present: C ∧ (T ∨ O). With C=true, T=false and O=true, the condition is true.
cs-u3-conditions.takeaway: The learner can distinguish a requirement, its converse and an implementation condition.

cs-u3-equivalence.title: Equivalence and Boolean algebra
cs-u3-equivalence.body: Equivalent formulas agree on every assignment. A valid formula is true on every assignment; a satisfiable formula is true on at least one. To disprove equivalence, one differing assignment suffices. Useful laws include ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q, ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q, and P ⇒ Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q. The symbol ≡ here means equivalence across assignments, not an extra program operator.
cs-u3-equivalence.example: ¬(Ready ∨ Busy) is equivalent to ¬Ready ∧ ¬Busy: both original flags must be false. Checking just one assignment would not establish this equivalence.
cs-u3-equivalence.takeaway: The learner can justify simplification by a law or a complete truth table.

cs-u3-normal-forms.title: Truth tables and normal forms
cs-u3-normal-forms.body: A literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. DNF is an OR of terms, each an AND of literals. CNF is an AND of clauses, each an OR of literals. To build a full DNF over fixed variables, write one term for each true row, mentioning every variable with the sign that selects that row. An n-variable truth table has 2^n rows. Form conversion can expand a short formula substantially.
cs-u3-normal-forms.example: For variables X,Y, a formula true only at (true,false) has full DNF X ∧ ¬Y. If (false,true) is also a true row, add the term ¬X ∧ Y using OR.
cs-u3-normal-forms.takeaway: The learner can connect a formula representation to its complete set of satisfying rows.

cs-u3-sat.title: SAT as a consistency check
cs-u3-sat.body: SAT asks whether there is any assignment making a propositional formula true. For constraints joined by AND, one assignment must satisfy every constraint simultaneously. A witness proves satisfiability; one failed trial does not prove impossibility. Unsatisfiability needs an exhaustive finite check or a valid argument. F is valid exactly when ¬F is unsatisfiable. A witness can be checked by evaluating the formula; finding one is a different task.
cs-u3-sat.example: Constraints K ⇒ L and K ∧ ¬L cannot both hold: the second makes K true and L false, which violates the first. This contradiction proves the conjunction unsatisfiable.
cs-u3-sat.takeaway: The learner can distinguish a witness, a failed trial, and an impossibility argument.

cs-u3-quantifiers.title: Predicates, domains and quantifiers
cs-u3-quantifiers.body: A predicate becomes a truth-valued claim once its free variables are assigned or quantified. ∀x∈D means every element of D; ∃x∈D means at least one, not exactly one. A restricted universal usually uses implication: ∀x∈D (Eligible(x) ⇒ Ready(x)). A restricted existential uses conjunction: ∃x∈D (Eligible(x) ∧ Ready(x)). For an explicitly empty D, the universal is true and the existential false. As in the book, an omitted discourse domain is assumed nonempty.
cs-u3-quantifiers.example: If Jobs={j1,j2} and only j2 is queued, “some job is queued” is true with witness j2. “Every job is queued” is false with counterexample j1.
cs-u3-quantifiers.takeaway: The learner can state the domain and distinguish a witness from a universal guarantee.

cs-u3-nested.title: Quantifier order and dependent witnesses
cs-u3-nested.body: In ∀x∈A ∃y∈B R(x,y), the chosen y may depend on x. In ∃y∈B ∀x∈A R(x,y), one y must work for every x. A common witness gives a per-input witness, but the converse need not hold. Swapping two universal quantifiers or two existential quantifiers preserves meaning; swapping different kinds generally does not. Parentheses and domains make the scope explicit.
cs-u3-nested.example: Two files f1,f2 have separate replicas: R(f1,s1) and R(f2,s2), with no other replica pairs. Every file has a server, but no single server stores both files.
cs-u3-nested.takeaway: The learner can test a quantifier claim against a small relation rather than rely on ambiguous English.

cs-u3-negation.title: Negating specifications and finding countermodels
cs-u3-negation.body: Negation swaps ∀ and ∃ and negates the predicate: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Apply this one quantifier at a time. Negating an implication gives a true premise and false conclusion. A formula with predicates is valid only if it holds for every allowed domain and interpretation; a single countermodel refutes validity.
cs-u3-negation.example: Negating “Every client has an available route” gives “Some client has no available route”: ¬[∀c∈C ∃r∈R A(c,r)] ≡ ∃c∈C ∀r∈R ¬A(c,r).
cs-u3-negation.takeaway: The learner can describe the exact witness or countermodel required by a failed specification.

cs-u4-sets.title: Sets, membership and exact collections
cs-u4-sets.body: A set ignores order and repeated listings. x∈A means x is an element; B⊆A means every element of B belongs to A. The empty set ∅ is a subset of every set. The set {∅} has one element and is not empty. Set-builder notation {x∈D | P(x)} filters a domain by a predicate. The power set pow(A) contains all subsets of A, including ∅ and A itself.
cs-u4-sets.example: If Flags={read,write}, then {read}⊆Flags and {read}∈pow(Flags). The string read is an element of Flags; the singleton set {read} is a different object.
cs-u4-sets.takeaway: The learner avoids element/subset and empty-container errors before manipulating collections.

cs-u4-set-algebra.title: Set operations and membership proofs
cs-u4-set-algebra.body: Union ∪ corresponds to OR of membership; intersection ∩ to AND. A\B contains elements of A absent from B. A complement must name its universe U: U\A. To prove A=B, show that an arbitrary x belongs to A iff it belongs to B, or prove both inclusions. One-sided inclusion does not establish equality. Logic operates on truth values; set operations operate on sets.
cs-u4-set-algebra.example: With U={a,b,c,d}, A={a,b} and B={b,c}, A∩B={b}, A\B={a}, and U\(A∪B)={d}.
cs-u4-set-algebra.takeaway: The learner connects Unit 3 logic to typed set reasoning and can exhibit a failing element.

cs-u4-sequences.title: Sequences, tuples and Cartesian products
cs-u4-sequences.body: A sequence preserves order and repetitions. A tuple is a finite sequence; equal tuples have the same length and equal components at each position. A×B is the set of ordered pairs (a,b) with a∈A and b∈B. It is usually different from B×A. S^n contains length-n sequences over S. S^0 contains one sequence, the empty sequence, even when S is empty.
cs-u4-sequences.example: For Method={GET,POST} and Status={200,500}, Method×Status has four pairs. (GET,500) is one pair, not the whole product; reversing it gives a differently typed record.
cs-u4-sequences.takeaway: The learner can reason about product types without losing order, multiplicity or the empty case.

cs-u4-functions.title: Functions, support and composition
cs-u4-functions.body: Following this edition, f:A→B may be partial: each a has at most one value in B. Its support contains inputs where it is defined; f is total when support(f)=A. Its range contains values actually produced, which may be fewer than the codomain B. Composition applies the right-hand function first: (g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)). For partial functions it is defined only if f(x) exists and belongs to support(g).
cs-u4-functions.example: Let f:Z→Z be f(x)=x+2 and g:Z→Z be g(x)=3x, both total. Then (g∘f)(1)=9 whereas (f∘g)(1)=5. Order matters.
cs-u4-functions.takeaway: The learner can distinguish a declared input type from supported inputs and actually produced outputs.

cs-u4-relations.title: Relations and mapping properties
cs-u4-relations.body: A relation from A to B specifies a graph contained in A×B. It may relate one input to several outputs. Functional means at most one output per input; total means at least one. Injective means at most one input per output, and surjective means at least one. In the book these properties also apply to relations that are not functions. A bijection has exactly one output per input and exactly one input per output. Changing A or B can change these properties.
cs-u4-relations.example: From A={p,q} to B={1,2,3}, graph {(p,1),(q,2)} is a total injective function, but not surjective because 3 is not reached.
cs-u4-relations.takeaway: The learner classifies mappings using all declared endpoints, including isolated ones.

cs-u4-images.title: Images, inverse images and inverse relations
cs-u4-images.body: For a relation R:A→B, R(S) collects outputs related to some input in S⊆A. The inverse relation R^(-1) reverses every pair. Its image R^(-1)(T) collects inputs related to some output in T⊆B: the inverse image, or preimage. This is defined even if R is not bijective. For a function, its inverse relation is functional exactly when the original function is injective; it is a total inverse function on B when the original is a bijection.
cs-u4-images.example: If f(a)=red, f(b)=red and f(c)=blue, then f({a,c})={red,blue} and f^(-1)({red})={a,b}. There is no unique inverse value at red, but its preimage set is perfectly defined.
cs-u4-images.takeaway: The learner can query mappings in either direction while preserving single-valuedness constraints.

cs-u4-cardinality.title: Finite cardinality and reversible encodings
cs-u4-cardinality.body: For finite sets, a total injective function A→B requires |A|≤|B|; a surjective function requires |A|≥|B|. A bijection proves equal sizes. If |A|=|B| and f is total, injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent. Totality matters: a partial injection can leave inputs unsupported. For a fixed ordered list of n distinct elements, each subset corresponds to its n-bit membership vector, so the power set has 2^n members.
cs-u4-cardinality.example: For ordered fields (id,name,age), subset {id,age} corresponds to vector (1,0,1). Every subset has one vector and every vector specifies one subset, giving a bijection.
cs-u4-cardinality.takeaway: The learner can justify finite size claims and explain when a collision-free encoding is impossible.

cs-u5-ordinary.title: Ordinary induction and the proof contract
cs-u5-ordinary.body: To prove P(n) for every integer n≥n0, establish P(n0), then fix an arbitrary k≥n0 and prove P(k)⇒P(k+1). In the step, P(k) is a temporary assumption for proving an implication; assuming P(k+1) would be circular. The argument must work for every allowed k. An empty sum is 0. Induction verifies a proposed formula; it does not automatically discover one.
cs-u5-ordinary.example: A buffer begins with capacity C(0)=5 and grows by 3 each step: C(n+1)=C(n)+3. Claim C(n)=5+3n. Base: C(0)=5. Step: assuming C(k)=5+3k gives C(k+1)=5+3k+3=5+3(k+1).
cs-u5-ordinary.takeaway: The learner can identify the base, hypothesis, target and quantification of a valid induction proof.

cs-u5-bounds.title: Induction for exponential bounds
cs-u5-bounds.body: An inequality proof needs a bridge from the bound available at k to the bound required at k+1. Multiplying by a positive quantity preserves direction; a negative multiplier reverses it. Verify the bridge on the entire induction range. A true base and a failed proof strategy do not establish that the theorem is false. Use exact mathematical integers here, without overflow.
cs-u5-bounds.example: To prove 2^n≥n+1 for n≥0: the base is 1≥1. If 2^k≥k+1, then 2^(k+1)≥2(k+1)≥k+2 because k≥0. The final expression is the next target.
cs-u5-bounds.takeaway: The learner can distinguish a numerical base check from the range condition supporting a general step.

cs-u5-strengthening.title: Strengthening the induction hypothesis
cs-u5-strengthening.body: A weak induction hypothesis may omit information needed to advance. Prove a stronger predicate Q(n) that implies the original goal, with its own base and step. Stronger must still be true. A common engineering pattern is a coupled update: proving a property of one quantity requires tracking a second quantity. Strengthening the predicate is different from strong induction, which allows earlier indices.
cs-u5-strengthening.example: Let u(0)=1, v(0)=2, u(n+1)=u(n)+v(n), and v(n+1)=2u(n)+v(n). To prove u(n)>0, use the stronger claim u(n)>0 and v(n)>0. Both updated values are then positive; tracking u alone does not directly bound v.
cs-u5-strengthening.takeaway: The learner can choose a useful auxiliary fact and check that it is established, not merely assumed.

cs-u5-strong.title: Strong induction for smaller subproblems
cs-u5-strong.body: Strong induction for n≥n0 permits assuming P(j) for every n0≤j<n when proving P(n). This helps when a subproblem is smaller but not exactly n-1. Every use of the hypothesis must satisfy that range. Handle terminal inputs explicitly. All arithmetic is exact, floor(x) is the greatest integer ≤x, and the integer recursions here are distinct from structural induction, reserved for Unit 7.
cs-u5-strong.example: For n≥1, a procedure stops at n=1 and otherwise recurses on floor(n/2). For n≥2, 1≤floor(n/2)<n. Strong induction therefore proves termination: the recursive call is covered by a smaller terminating case.
cs-u5-strong.takeaway: The learner can apply the induction hypothesis only to legitimate smaller inputs.

cs-u5-bases.title: Multiple base cases and dependency gaps
cs-u5-bases.body: A recurrence using n-2 and n-3 needs enough directly established cases before both dependencies lie in range. Likewise, a step P(k)⇒P(k+d) only moves within a residue class modulo d; one base may leave whole classes uncovered. The number of bases is determined by the proof’s dependencies and starting range, not a universal rule. Inspect the earliest inductive transition carefully.
cs-u5-bases.example: If P(k)⇒P(k+3) for every k≥0, proving P(0), P(1) and P(2) starts all three chains: 0,3,6,...; 1,4,7,...; and 2,5,8,.... P(0) alone starts only the first chain.
cs-u5-bases.takeaway: The learner can explain why base coverage is sufficient instead of checking an arbitrary number of examples.

cs-u5-principles.title: Induction, well-ordering and proof review
cs-u5-principles.body: Ordinary induction, strong induction and well-ordering over the nonnegative integers have equivalent proving power. To package strong induction as ordinary induction, use Q(n): “P(j) holds for every 0≤j≤n.” Conversely, if a base and successor step hold but a counterexample exists, well-ordering gives a least counterexample m. The base excludes m=0, so P(m-1) and the step force P(m), a contradiction. Equivalence of methods does not repair a missing premise.
cs-u5-principles.example: Suppose P(0) and every successor implication hold. A least failing index m cannot be 0. Minimality gives P(m-1); the successor implication then gives P(m). Thus no failing index exists.
cs-u5-principles.takeaway: The learner can audit an induction proof and connect it to minimal-counterexample reasoning.
